title: AI agents are not good at interpreting science. What can be done?
source_used: Chemical & Engineering News (C&EN), read in full
key_facts: Valentin Rodionov, an organic chemist at Case Western Reserve University, chose 42 studies that do not meet the standards of legitimate research: some retracted, others problematic or fraudulent but not formally retracted.
He uploaded sections of the papers to 30 AI models, 10 times each, mostly large language models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Google, Mistral AI and others.
In his paper, posted on arXiv in August, the models on average uncritically suggested building on the flawed research around 93% of the time.
The 42 studies include the retracted paper linking the MMR vaccine to autism, a retracted 2008 tracheal transplant paper by the disgraced surgeon Paolo Macchiarini, and a debunked cold fusion report.
Claude Sonnet 5 scored best of the 30 models, but still engaged with or created study designs based on bad science about 72% of the time.
The best tools acknowledged that something was controversial about the subject around half the time.

Proposals include Nicholas Peoples's team's 'digital sim cards' in study metadata, Peter Koo's 'uncertainty layer', and a verifier that AI companies could build in; Rodionov has launched a company, Intellicat, that sells AI companies a 'content credibility index'.
quote_evidence: AI should not be promoting pseudoscience, conspiracy theories, and things that are detrimental to public health.
If the general public tries to engage with research, and if the large language model does not provide appropriate nuances or caveats, then it could lead to the public getting misled.
Incorrect interpretation of scientific data is a core problem in science.
why_it_matters_hint: People who use AI to read science may get confident support for false or retracted work, which matters for clinical guidance and public trust.
event_date: Aug 2026 (preprint posted on arXiv; exact day not stated); C&EN feature 7 Oct 2026
notes: Full text read. The underlying study is a preprint posted on arXiv in August 2026 (older news re-dated; the C&EN feature is new). Pool score lowered by 1 (6 to 5) for that reason. Named people with position: Valentin Rodionov (organic chemist, Case Western Reserve University); Nihar Shah (computer scientist, Carnegie Mellon University); Nicholas Peoples (resident physician in emergency medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital); Peter Koo (quantitative biologist, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory).
